title: Tasks, microtasks, and event loop
learningObjectives: Distinguish synchronous execution, the call stack, tasks and microtasks.
Predict ordering of Promise reactions, queueMicrotask callbacks and timer callbacks.
Explain that a microtask checkpoint drains the microtask queue, including newly queued microtasks.
Explain how long tasks and unbounded microtask chains delay other work and rendering opportunities.
Apply event-loop knowledge when debugging asynchronous browser code.

understand.concept: Synchronous JavaScript runs on the call stack. When the current stack is empty, the host environment coordinates queued work through the event loop. In browsers, timer callbacks and many user events are tasks. Promise reactions and queueMicrotask callbacks are microtasks. At a microtask checkpoint, the queue is processed until empty, including microtasks added by other microtasks. The browser can then proceed with other event-loop work and may render at an appropriate point. A zero-delay timer does not run immediately; it makes a callback eligible as a future task. Rendering opportunities are controlled by the browser and are not guaranteed after every callback.
understand.whyItMatters: This model explains callback ordering, why timers are not precise clocks, and why heavy synchronous work freezes an interface. An endless microtask chain can also postpone other tasks and rendering opportunities. These details matter when debugging responsive interfaces, asynchronous requests, race conditions and UI updates.
understand.analogy: Tasks are scheduled jobs; microtasks are follow-up work that must be cleared before the next scheduled job is selected.
understand.analogyLimit: The analogy is simplified. Browser scheduling includes task sources, rendering lifecycle and host-specific behaviour; do not infer that every callback is a task or that a paint must happen after each task.

explain.narrative: The current synchronous stack finishes first. Promise.then and queueMicrotask schedule microtasks. At the next microtask checkpoint, queued microtasks run in order; a microtask that queues another microtask adds work to the same checkpoint. Once the queue is empty, the event loop can select another task, such as an eligible timer callback. An async function runs synchronously until it suspends at await; its continuation resumes asynchronously. Avoid endless microtask chains because they can starve tasks. Do not assume the browser paints after every individual callback.

examples.explanation: Synchronous statements finish first. Microtasks then run in queue order. The timer callback runs as a later task; zero delay does not mean immediate execution.
examples.expectedOutput:
sync start
sync end
queued microtask
promise reaction
timer task

examples.explanation: The first reaction queues microtask 3. The checkpoint continues until all microtasks, including newly queued ones, have run.
An async function begins synchronously. Its continuation after await is scheduled asynchronously, so the caller continues first.
Each microtask queues another. The checkpoint drains this finite chain before the timer task. An unbounded chain can prevent the event loop from progressing.

practise.guidedTask: Predict the output of examples 1-3 before running them. Add one nested queueMicrotask call and explain why it runs before the next timer task.
practise.independentTask: Build a small interaction that logs a click handler, a Promise continuation and a timer callback. Add loading and completion states. Explain which code is synchronous, which callbacks are microtasks, which are tasks, and why rendering is not guaranteed after every callback.
hints: Promise reactions and queueMicrotask callbacks are microtasks.
A microtask can queue another microtask in the same checkpoint.
setTimeout with zero delay is still a future task.
An async function runs until it reaches await, then resumes asynchronously.
Long synchronous tasks and endless microtask chains both harm responsiveness.

questions.prompt: Which runs before the event loop selects the next task after the synchronous stack is empty?
questions.explanation: Microtasks are processed at the checkpoint before the next task is selected.
Promise reactions and queueMicrotask enqueue microtasks; timer callbacks are tasks.

questions.prompt: A microtask queues another microtask. When can the new callback run?
options: During the same checkpoint after earlier queued work
questions.answer: During the same checkpoint after earlier queued work
questions.explanation: The microtask queue is drained until empty, including newly queued microtasks.

options: The callback becomes eligible as a future task
The callback interrupts current synchronous code
The callback runs before Promise reactions
questions.answer: The callback becomes eligible as a future task
questions.explanation: A zero delay does not make the callback synchronous or immediate.

questions.prompt: What happens when an async function reaches await?
options: Its continuation resumes asynchronously and the caller can continue
The function becomes a timer task
questions.answer: Its continuation resumes asynchronously and the caller can continue
questions.explanation: The async function suspends at await and resumes through Promise scheduling.

questions.prompt: Why can an endless microtask chain harm responsiveness?
options: It can prevent the event loop from selecting other tasks and reaching rendering opportunities
It moves work to a worker automatically
questions.answer: It can prevent the event loop from selecting other tasks and reaching rendering opportunities
questions.explanation: The checkpoint is drained before another task is selected.
